short_description: Heart health describes how well your heart and blood vessels are likely to keep working over time. This assessment estimates your risk of heart and blood vessel disease.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Your heart pumps blood through a network of blood vessels to every part of your body.
Over years, cholesterol can build up as plaque inside artery walls, and high blood pressure can stiffen them.
Narrowed or blocked arteries can reduce blood flow to the heart or brain, which can lead to a heart attack or stroke.
why_it_matters: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of illness and death, and it often develops silently for years.
Many of its main drivers, such as blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar and smoking, can be checked and managed.

short_description: Cholesterol imbalance, also called dyslipidaemia, means the fats in your blood, such as cholesterol and triglycerides, are at unhealthy levels.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Your blood carries fats inside particles such as LDL, HDL and VLDL.
Too much LDL or triglycerides, or too little HDL, makes it easier for fatty plaque to build up in arteries.
The build-up happens slowly and usually without symptoms.
why_it_matters: Unhealthy blood fats are one of the main causes of heart attacks and strokes.
Unhealthy blood fats can be found with a simple blood test and are often improved with lifestyle and, when needed, treatment.

short_description: High blood pressure, or hypertension, means blood is pushing too hard against the walls of your arteries for a long time.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Blood pressure is the force of blood on artery walls as your heart pumps.
When it stays high, the heart works harder and artery walls become strained and stiff.
Over time this damages blood vessels in the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes.
why_it_matters: High blood pressure is very common and is a leading cause of stroke, heart attack and kidney disease.
High blood pressure usually has no symptoms, so measuring it is the only way to know.

short_description: Fatty liver means extra fat has built up inside your liver cells. The common form is now called MASLD, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, which replaced the older name NAFLD.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Your liver stores some fat, but too much can build up when the body takes in more energy than it uses.

Doctors call it MASLD when fat in the liver comes with metabolic risk factors, such as a large waist or extra weight, high blood sugar or type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, or high triglycerides or low HDL, and is not caused by heavy alcohol use.
When fat in the liver comes with inflammation and liver cell damage, it is called MASH, which replaced the older name NASH. Over years this can lead to scarring.
why_it_matters: Fatty liver is very common and often silent.
Fatty liver is closely linked with type 2 diabetes, high triglycerides and heart disease, and early stages can improve with lifestyle change.

short_description: Type 2 diabetes is a long-term condition where blood sugar stays too high, because the body does not respond well to insulin or does not make enough of it.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Insulin is a hormone that moves sugar from your blood into your cells for energy.

The pancreas works harder to make more insulin, and over time it may not keep up, so blood sugar rises.
why_it_matters: Type 2 diabetes is very common, especially in South Asia, and can develop silently for years.
Finding risk early allows changes that can delay or prevent it.

short_description: Thyroid health describes how well your thyroid gland, a small butterfly-shaped gland in your neck, is making the hormones that set your body's pace.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Your thyroid makes hormones called T4 and T3 that control how fast your body uses energy.
A signal from your brain, called TSH, tells the thyroid how much to make.
If the thyroid makes too little or too much, many body systems slow down or speed up.
why_it_matters: Thyroid problems are common, especially in women, and can affect energy, weight, mood, periods, fertility and the heart.
Thyroid problems are easy to check with a blood test and usually treatable.

relevant_lifestyle_factors.association: Your thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones. Iodised salt can supply iodine.

common_misconceptions: Thyroid problems are not usually caused by diet.

clinical_limitations: A predicted risk does not measure your thyroid hormones. Only blood tests can show how your thyroid is working.

Pregnancy changes thyroid needs, and some women develop thyroid inflammation after childbirth.
Medicines such as lithium and amiodarone can affect the thyroid.
Thyroid conditions are much more common in women and become more common with age.

keeping_healthy: Thyroid conditions are not usually prevented by habits. Knowing the symptoms and having thyroid tests when advised, especially in pregnancy or with a family history, is what helps.

short_description: An underactive thyroid, or hypothyroidism, means your thyroid gland is not making enough hormone, so many body processes slow down.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Thyroid hormones set how fast your cells use energy.
When there is too little hormone, the brain sends more TSH to push the thyroid harder.
The most common cause is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, where the immune system slowly damages the thyroid.
why_it_matters: An underactive thyroid is common, especially in women, and can affect energy, weight, mood, cholesterol, periods and pregnancy.
common_misconceptions: Weight gain from an underactive thyroid is usually modest.
Eating cabbage or soya in normal amounts does not cause thyroid disease.
clinical_limitations: A predicted risk does not measure your thyroid hormones. Blood tests are needed.

long_term_implications: Untreated, it can raise cholesterol, affect the heart, and cause problems with fertility and pregnancy.
when_to_seek_medical_advice: Talk to a doctor if your predicted risk is increased or very high, or if you have symptoms. A TSH test is the main check. Treatment, if needed, is a daily tablet decided by a doctor.

Treatments that remove or reduce the thyroid can leave it underactive.
Lithium and amiodarone can make the thyroid underactive.

keeping_healthy: Thyroid conditions are not usually prevented by habits. Knowing the symptoms and having thyroid tests when advised, especially in pregnancy or with a family history, is what helps.

short_description: An overactive thyroid, or hyperthyroidism, means your thyroid gland is making too much hormone, so many body processes speed up.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Too much thyroid hormone makes cells use energy faster.
The brain's TSH signal falls in response.
The most common cause is Graves' disease, where the immune system pushes the thyroid to overwork.
why_it_matters: An overactive thyroid can strain the heart, thin the bones and cause pregnancy problems if not treated.
common_misconceptions: Weight loss from an overactive thyroid is not healthy weight loss.
clinical_limitations: A predicted risk does not measure your thyroid hormones. Blood tests are needed.
suggested_questions: What does my overactive thyroid risk mean?
What are the signs of an overactive thyroid?
Can my thyroid cause a racing heart?
Should I get my thyroid checked?

relevant_biomarker_context.reason: Shows T3, which is often high when the thyroid is overactive.
Shows T4, which is often high when the thyroid is overactive.
Shows TSH, which usually falls when the thyroid is overactive.

common_symptoms: Weight loss, a fast or irregular heartbeat, feeling hot, sweating, shaky hands, anxiety, poor sleep and frequent bowel movements.
influencing_factors_note: These are known general influences on this area of health. They are not confirmed inputs to, or reasons for, your own score.
diet_and_lifestyle: An overactive thyroid is mainly caused by the immune system rather than habits. Very high iodine intake, for example from some supplements, can trigger it in some people.
long_term_implications: Untreated, it can cause an irregular heart rhythm, heart strain and thinning bones.
when_to_seek_medical_advice: Talk to a doctor if your predicted risk is increased or very high, or you have symptoms. Seek care promptly for a racing or irregular heartbeat, chest pain or severe shakiness.

It is not a diagnosis and does not measure the condition directly.
MetSights has not published the exact outcome each score predicts, over what time, or how the band is calculated, so CURA does not turn it into a percentage chance.

not_applicable.practical_guidance: An overactive thyroid needs medical treatment; no everyday habit reliably helps it.

factor_explanations.how_it_acts: The commonest cause: antibodies stimulate the thyroid to make too much hormone.
Lumps in the thyroid can make hormone on their own.
Taking more levothyroxine than you need has the same effect as an overactive gland.
Inflammation, including after childbirth or a viral illness, can release stored hormone for a while.
Iodine-rich medicines or contrast dye can trigger an overactive thyroid in some people.
It is more common in women and runs in families.

keeping_healthy: Thyroid conditions are not usually prevented by habits. Knowing the symptoms and having thyroid tests when advised, especially in pregnancy or with a family history, is what helps.

short_description: Polycystic ovary syndrome, or PCOS, is a common hormone condition that can make periods irregular, raise male-type hormones and affect how the body handles sugar.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Normally the ovaries release an egg each month.
In PCOS, hormone signals shift, so eggs may not be released regularly and periods become irregular.
The ovaries may make more androgens, male-type hormones that can cause acne or extra hair growth.
Many people with PCOS also have insulin resistance, which can raise blood sugar and weight.
why_it_matters: PCOS is one of the most common hormone conditions in women of reproductive age.
PCOS can affect periods, fertility, skin, mood and long-term metabolic health.
relevant_lifestyle_factors: Moving more often and including vegetables, pulses, fruit and unsweetened drinks can support insulin sensitivity.
Sleep and stress matter for hormones, but a habit does not by itself cause a PCOS score.
Weight can be associated with PCOS. It is not the cause for everyone, and a prediction does not say a person's eating caused it.
common_misconceptions: You can have PCOS even if your weight is normal.
Not everyone with PCOS has cysts on the ovaries, and ovarian cysts alone do not mean PCOS.
PCOS and PCOD are commonly used names for the same condition.
No single blood test confirms PCOS.
A predicted PCOS band is not a diagnosis. Only a doctor can diagnose PCOS, using your periods, signs of high male-type hormones (androgens), blood tests and sometimes an ultrasound.
clinical_limitations: A doctor diagnoses PCOS from your periods, signs of high male-type hormones (androgens), blood tests and sometimes an ultrasound.
suggested_questions: What does my PCOS score mean?
Can I have PCOS even if my weight is normal?
How are PCOS and blood sugar connected?
When should I see a doctor about PCOS?

relevant_biomarker_context.reason: Shows testosterone, a male-type hormone that is often higher in PCOS.
Shows LH, a hormone that controls egg release and can be raised in PCOS.
Shows FSH, which helps eggs develop and is read with LH.
Shows your fasting blood sugar, which PCOS can affect.
Shows fasting insulin, which is often high with insulin resistance in PCOS.

everyday_support: Build regular movement into your week, including some strength exercise. Activity helps your body respond to insulin.
Base meals on vegetables, protein and whole grains, and limit sugary drinks and sweets. Steadier blood sugar can help hormone balance.
Keep a regular sleep routine and find ways to manage stress. Both affect hormones and insulin.
Track your periods in a calendar or app. It helps your doctor understand your pattern.
common_symptoms: Acne, oily skin, extra facial or body hair, or hair thinning on the scalp.
Weight gain or difficulty losing weight, and difficulty getting pregnant.
influencing_factors_note: These are known general influences on this area of health. They are not confirmed inputs to, or reasons for, your own score.
diet_and_lifestyle: Regular activity, balanced meals and healthy sleep help insulin work better, which can improve PCOS symptoms.
PCOS also occurs in people of normal weight.
long_term_implications: PCOS is linked with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, high cholesterol, fatty liver, sleep apnoea, low mood and, with very infrequent periods, thickening of the womb lining.
when_to_seek_medical_advice: Talk to a doctor if your predicted risk is increased or very high, or if you have irregular periods, acne or extra hair growth, or difficulty getting pregnant.
See a doctor if you go three months or more without a period and are not pregnant.
risk_meaning: Your Bio-AI result is a risk band from MetSights' prediction model, built from your blood results and other information such as lifestyle answers.
It is not a diagnosis and does not measure the condition directly.
MetSights has not published the exact outcome each score predicts, over what time, or how the band is calculated, so CURA does not turn it into a percentage chance.

factor_explanations.how_it_acts: PCOS runs in families, and a mother or sister with PCOS or type 2 diabetes raises the chance.
High insulin pushes the ovaries to make more androgens, which disturbs ovulation.
Extra weight worsens insulin resistance and symptoms, though PCOS also occurs at normal weight.
Activity helps the body respond to insulin, which can ease symptoms.
Poor sleep and ongoing stress can worsen insulin resistance and cycle regularity.

keeping_healthy: Regular activity, meals that keep blood sugar steady and regular sleep support hormone and insulin balance, whatever your weight.

short_description: Oxidative stress is what happens when substances your cells make as they work build up faster than your body's protective systems can handle them.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Your cells naturally make some reactive molecules, often called free radicals, as they use energy.
Your body has protective systems, including antioxidants from food, that keep these molecules in balance.
When that protection cannot keep up, the extra molecules may damage parts of cells. That imbalance is called oxidative stress.
why_it_matters: Over time, this imbalance can affect the health of cells.
Research discusses oxidative stress alongside inflammation and some longer-term health conditions.
everyday_support: Include a variety of vegetables, fruit, pulses and other minimally processed foods. They provide natural antioxidants.
Keep a sleep routine that gives you enough rest. Sleep supports your body's repair processes.
Stay physically active in a way that fits your usual day. Regular moderate activity strengthens the body's own protective systems.
If you smoke, ask for help to stop. Smoking is a strong source of oxidative stress.
common_misconceptions: A normal blood report does not contradict a higher oxidative stress band, because routine blood tests do not measure it.
Antioxidant supplements have not been shown to prevent disease, and high-dose beta-carotene raised lung cancer risk in smokers.
This band is not a measurement of damage to your cells.
clinical_limitations: This score is a risk estimate, not a direct measurement of cell damage.
suggested_questions: Why is my oxidative stress risk high when a blood test in this area is normal?
Which everyday habits are linked with oxidative stress?
Which foods support the body's protective systems?
Do I need antioxidant supplements?

relevant_biomarker_context.reason: Shows hs-CRP, a sign of inflammation, which often goes alongside oxidative stress.
Shows vitamin C, one of the body's antioxidants from food.

common_symptoms: Oxidative stress does not cause symptoms you can feel.
influencing_factors_note: These are known general influences on this area of health. They are not confirmed inputs to, or reasons for, your own score.
diet_and_lifestyle: Smoking, heavy alcohol use, diets low in fruit and vegetables, and poor sleep are studied as general influences on oxidative stress.
long_term_implications: Research links long-term oxidative stress with inflammation and some conditions such as heart disease, but a score does not show that this has happened.
when_to_seek_medical_advice: There is no specific medical test or treatment for oxidative stress. Talk to a doctor if you have other raised risks or symptoms that worry you.
risk_meaning: Your Bio-AI result is a risk band from MetSights' prediction model, built from your blood results and other information such as lifestyle answers.
It is not a diagnosis and does not measure the condition directly.
MetSights has not published the exact outcome each score predicts, over what time, or how the band is calculated, so CURA does not turn it into a percentage chance.
Routine blood tests do not measure oxidative stress directly, and MetSights has not said exactly what this score predicts.

factor_explanations.how_it_acts: Vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains provide antioxidants that support the body's own protection.
Sleep supports the body's repair processes.
Exercise makes some free radicals, but regular moderate activity strengthens the body's own protective systems.
Smoke is one of the strongest outside sources of free radicals.
Long-term stress is linked with more oxidative strain.
Breaking down alcohol produces reactive molecules in the liver.
Pollution and ultraviolet light create free radicals in the lungs and skin.

keeping_healthy: Not smoking, a varied diet with plenty of vegetables, fruit and dal, regular moderate activity and enough sleep support the body's own protective systems.

short_description: Metabolic age is a Bio-AI estimate that MetSights presents as an age, to sum up parts of your metabolic health such as how your body handles sugar and fats. MetSights has not published how the number is calculated or what it is compared against.
product_inputs: MetSights can look at blood biomarkers, lifestyle, food, activity, sleep, demographics and other questionnaire answers when it builds risk scores and metabolic scores.
That is the known general input set. The formula, feature weights and reference population are not available, and not every answer feeds every score.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Metabolic health is how well your body turns food into energy, keeps blood sugar steady and handles fats.
Your actual age is how many years you have lived. Metabolic age is an estimate based on health information, not a count of birthdays.

MetSights has not shared the formula, the weight given to each input or the group it compares you with, so the gap between your metabolic age and your real age cannot be read as a precise measure of anything.
why_it_matters: Metabolic age is a simple way to start a conversation about blood sugar, blood fats, weight, activity and sleep.
The estimate does not measure how long you will live or how fast your whole body is ageing.
relevant_lifestyle_factors: Everyday movement, meals built around vegetables, pulses and unsweetened drinks, and regular sleep support metabolic health.
Those habits are discussed separately from the estimate unless a documented method says they contributed to it.
common_misconceptions: A higher metabolic age does not mean you have lost years of life.
A lower metabolic age does not guarantee good health.
Normal blood results can sit alongside a higher estimate, because a prediction is not a measurement.
No habit is promised to change the number by a set number of years.
Your measured results, such as HbA1c, fasting sugar and cholesterol, are a more reliable guide to where to focus than the metabolic age number.
clinical_limitations: The calculation method, inputs and reference group are not available, so CURA cannot say what produced your estimate.
suggested_questions: What does my metabolic age mean?
Can my metabolic age change over time?
How is metabolic age different from biological age?
What habits support my metabolic health?
everyday_support: Move regularly and include some strength exercise. Activity helps your body use sugar and fats.
Base meals on vegetables, pulses, whole grains and protein, with fewer sugary and fried foods. This supports steadier blood sugar and blood fats.
Keep a regular sleep routine. Enough sleep is part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance.
influencing_factors_note: These are known general influences on this area of health. They are not confirmed inputs to, or reasons for, your own score.
diet_and_lifestyle: Activity, eating habits, sleep and weight are general influences on metabolic health. The provider has not said which inputs or weights it uses.
long_term_implications: Metabolic age is not linked to a specific disease. Metabolic health in general is linked with the risk of diabetes, fatty liver and heart disease.
when_to_seek_medical_advice: There is no medical treatment for metabolic age itself. Talk to a doctor about any raised blood sugar, cholesterol or other risks shown alongside it.
risk_meaning: Metabolic age is an estimate from your Bio-AI assessment, not a measurement or diagnosis.
A different estimate on a later assessment can reflect changes in your health or in the information used.

not_applicable.symptoms: A prediction about metabolic patterns; it has no symptoms of its own.
not_applicable.blood_test_relationships: The provider has not published which blood tests feed this estimate.

factor_explanations.how_it_acts: Activity helps the body use sugar and fats well.
Meals built around vegetables, pulses and whole grains support steadier blood sugar and blood fats.
Enough sleep is part of the lifestyle that may help prevent insulin resistance.
Extra weight, especially around the waist, makes insulin and fat handling less efficient.
These are the measured parts of metabolic health that blood tests can show.

keeping_healthy: Regular activity, balanced meals and enough sleep support metabolic health. Your measured results show where attention will help most.
